flags.detail: The key (A, prints "B") is right and the first sentence of the explanation is right. The last sentence is not: "it would only become undefined if speak() were pure virtual with no definition, since there would then be no function to call." C++17 [class.abstract]/6 makes a virtual call to a pure virtual function from a constructor or destructor of an abstract class undefined *whether or not the pure virtual function has a definition* — the definition is only reachable through a qualified call, and providing one does not make the virtual call defined. The explanation as written teaches the reader that `struct B { B(){ speak(); } virtual void speak() = 0; }; void B::speak(){...}` is well-defined, which is exactly the UB-that-appears-to-work trap. I compiled both forms with g++ 13.3 -std=c++17. With an out-of-class definition (scratchpad ua_043b.cpp) the program printed "B-pure-def / survived" and exited 0, and printed the same under -fsanitize=undefined — i.e. the UB silently "works", which makes the false claim more dangerous, not less. Without a definition (ua_043c.cpp) GCC devirtualises the in-constructor call and the program does not even link: "undefined reference to `B::speak()'" — so the explanation's stated mechanism ("no function to call" at run time) is not what happens on the reference implementation either. Fix: replace the final clause with something like "it would become undefined if speak() were pure virtual, since a virtual call to a pure virtual function from a base constructor is undefined behaviour even when that function has an out-of-class definition." Keep key A.
flags.suggested: A (key unchanged); rewrite the last clause of the explanation to: "...it would only become undefined if speak() were declared pure virtual — a virtual call to a pure virtual function from a constructor of an abstract class is undefined behaviour under [class.abstract]/6, and supplying an out-of-class definition for it does not change that."

flags.detail: The key (B, std::length_error) is correct and I verified the whole hierarchy programmatically with std::is_base_of under g++ 13.3 (scratchpad ua_063.cpp): length_error derives from logic_error; range_error, overflow_error and system_error all derive from runtime_error. The defect is a header misattribution in the stem. The stem says "In the standard exception hierarchy of <stdexcept>", but option D, std::system_error, is not declared in <stdexcept> — it lives in <system_error>. Compiling a TU that includes only <stdexcept> and names std::system_error fails: "error: 'system_error' is not a member of 'std'" (ua_063b.cpp). A student who reads the stem literally learns a wrong header for system_error. It does not change the answer, hence low. Two clean fixes: either swap option D for std::underflow_error, which really is in <stdexcept> and really does derive from runtime_error (preserving the distractor's function), or reword the stem to "In the standard library's exception hierarchy" and drop the header claim.
flags.suggested: B (key unchanged); replace option D "std::system_error" with "std::underflow_error", or change the stem to "In the standard library's exception hierarchy, ..." and adjust the explanation's closing clause accordingly.
